questions.q: Why can't standard backpropagation be used to train a variational circuit running on real quantum hardware?
options: Real hardware only provides measurement outcomes from full circuit evaluations -- you cannot inspect or differentiate intermediate internal states mid-execution
Backpropagation only works for classification tasks, never regression
Quantum circuits have no parameters that could be differentiated
Backpropagation requires more than 2 qubits to function at all
questions.explain: Backprop needs access to intermediate computation steps. Real hardware gives you only full-circuit measurement outcomes with no way to inspect internal states mid-circuit, which is exactly why a different gradient method -- the parameter-shift rule -- is needed.

questions.q: For the circuit f(theta) = cos(theta) at theta = pi/3, what does the parameter-shift rule [f(theta+pi/2) - f(theta-pi/2)]/2 evaluate to?
options: Approximately -0.866, matching the analytic derivative -sin(pi/3)
Approximately 0.5, matching cos(pi/3) itself
Exactly 0, since the shifts cancel out
Approximately 1.0, the maximum possible expectation value
questions.explain: f(theta+pi/2)=cos(5pi/6)=-0.866 and f(theta-pi/2)=cos(-pi/6)=0.866; (-0.866-0.866)/2 = -0.866, which exactly matches the calculus derivative -sin(pi/3) = -0.866.

questions.q: Why is the parameter-shift rule's shift of exactly pi/2 fundamentally different from a classical finite-difference step size epsilon?
options: Pi/2 is an exact value determined by the gate's eigenvalue structure, giving an EXACT gradient -- not an approximation that improves as epsilon shrinks toward zero like classical finite differences
Pi/2 is simply the smallest step size that still fits on NISQ hardware
There is no difference; pi/2 is just a conventional default epsilon value
Classical finite differences also use exactly pi/2 as their step size
questions.explain: Parameter-shift is exact at pi/2 for Pauli-generated rotation gates, not an approximation that gets better as the step shrinks -- unlike classical finite differences, which only approximate the true derivative and get noisier as epsilon shrinks on real hardware.

questions.q: How many full circuit evaluations does the parameter-shift rule require to compute the gradient for a circuit with k trainable parameters?
options: 2k evaluations -- two shifted evaluations per parameter
k evaluations total, one per parameter
1 evaluation regardless of k, same as classical backprop
k^2 evaluations, growing quadratically
questions.explain: Each parameter needs its own plus-shift and minus-shift evaluation, giving 2k total circuit evaluations for a full gradient -- a real practical bottleneck compared to classical backprop's roughly single-extra-pass cost regardless of parameter count.

questions.q: For g(theta) = sin(theta), what is the parameter-shift gradient at theta = pi/2, and does it match the calculus derivative g'(theta) = cos(theta) at that point?
options: g(pi) = 0 and g(0) = 0, giving gradient 0, matching cos(pi/2) = 0
g(pi) = 1 and g(0) = 1, giving gradient 1, matching cos(pi/2) = 1
g(pi) = -1 and g(0) = 1, giving gradient -1, not matching cos(pi/2)
The parameter-shift rule cannot be applied to sin(theta) at all
questions.explain: sin(pi/2+pi/2)=sin(pi)=0 and sin(pi/2-pi/2)=sin(0)=0, so the gradient is (0-0)/2=0, which exactly matches cos(pi/2)=0 -- confirming the rule works for this case too.
